headline: Europe considers keeping young children off social media

sources.title: EU to limit children's access to social media
EU plans to ban under-13s from social media, with 'phased access' afterwards
EU chief weighs age restrictions for children using social media
Podcast | Is social media over for under -13s in the EU? (video, euronews)

chunks.text: A [[growing number of]] governments are trying to {{clamp down}} on children's use of social media. The trend {{kicked off}} in Australia, which {{rolled out}} a [[ban]] on the apps for anyone under 16. Now the European Union is thinking about a similar [[policy]] for the young people in its [[member countries]]. Leaders say the plan is [[meant to]] protect [[minors]] from [[harm]].

verbs.correct: To take strong action to stop or control something
verbs.wrong: To punish people who have already broken an existing rule
verbs.why: Clamp down means to take firm, official action to control or stop a problem. More governments are trying to clamp down on how children use social media apps.

verbs.correct: To start or begin an event or activity
verbs.why: Kick off means to start something, often in a noticeable or public way. This trend of limiting children's social media use kicked off in Australia, with a ban for anyone under 16.

verbs.correct: To officially start or introduce something new
verbs.wrong: To slowly cancel a rule that is no longer needed
verbs.why: Roll out means to officially introduce a new rule or product to the public. Australia rolled out a ban on social media apps for anyone under 16 years old.

chunks.text: Under the new idea, children under 13 would not be able to {{sign up}} for social media at all. After that age, teenagers would [[gradually]] be allowed to join, but only [[once]] the [[platforms]] {{carry out}} stronger safety checks. Ursula von der Leyen, who {{heads up}} the European Commission, said the plan is not about stopping children from using the apps. She said it is really about deciding when the apps can [[reach into]] children's lives.

verbs.correct: To join or register for a service or activity
verbs.wrong: To formally agree to follow a set of rules
verbs.why: Sign up means to register as a member of a service or platform. Under the new plan, children under 13 could not sign up for social media at all.

verbs.correct: To do or perform a task, often one that was planned
verbs.wrong: To keep doing an activity in the same way as before
verbs.why: Carry out is a formal way to say do something, especially a plan or a check. Platforms must carry out stronger safety checks before older teenagers are allowed to join.

verbs.correct: To be the leader of a group or organization
verbs.wrong: To speak for a group as its main voice
verbs.why: Head up means to be the leader in charge of an organization or a team. Ursula von der Leyen heads up the European Commission, which is behind this proposal.

chunks.text: People who support the rules [[point to]] studies that connect [[heavy]] app use with worse [[mental health]] [[among]] teenagers. They [[argue]] that the apps are built to {{draw in}} young users and keep them scrolling for hours. To deal with this, the EU may make companies {{turn off}} features like [[autoplay]] and [[endless]] scrolling. Many parents also worry about the anxiety and lost sleep that come with [[constant]] use.

verbs.correct: To attract someone and get their interest
verbs.wrong: To trap someone so that they cannot escape
verbs.why: Draw in means to attract people and pull their attention toward something. Critics argue that social media apps are built to draw in young users and keep them scrolling.

verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.wrong: To remove something completely and permanently
verbs.why: Turn off means to switch a feature or function so that it stops working. The EU may make companies turn off features like autoplay and endless scrolling for young users.

chunks.text: Not everyone {{goes along with}} the plans. Some experts warn that [[strict]] [[age checks]] could put everyone's [[privacy]] [[at risk]], [[since]] websites would need to gather more personal information. Others say a ban might {{shut out}} young people from useful advice, support groups, and online friends. The EU [[is expected to]] {{put forward}} a formal [[proposal]] after the summer break, and countries around the world are watching to see [[what happens next]].

verbs.correct: To agree with or support a plan or idea
verbs.wrong: To finally do something you promised to do
verbs.why: Go along with means to accept and support a plan, even without much enthusiasm. Not everyone goes along with the EU's plan, since some worry it could hurt privacy.

verbs.correct: To prevent someone from joining or getting in
verbs.wrong: To make someone feel unwelcome and unwanted
verbs.why: Shut out means to block someone from having access to something they need. A ban might shut out young people from useful advice, support groups, and online friends.

verbs.correct: To suggest or present a plan or idea to others
verbs.wrong: To quietly remove a plan from the discussion
verbs.why: Put forward means to formally present an idea or plan for others to consider. The EU is expected to put forward a formal proposal after the summer break.

mainIdea.s: The European Union is thinking about a plan to stop children under 13 from joining social media. Older teens could sign up later once platforms carry out stronger safety checks.
mainIdea.why: The story says under the new idea, children under 13 could not sign up at all. Teens could join later once platforms carry out stronger safety checks.

mainIdea.s: The European Union plans to shut out every teenager from social media until they turn eighteen. Leaders say the plan will end the apps completely across every member country.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the plan only covers children under 13. Teens can gradually join after that, once platforms carry out stronger safety checks.

mainIdea.s: Last year, several countries in Asia signed a deal to share health data between hospitals and clinics. Officials there said the plan would help doctors treat patients faster.
mainIdea.why: This story is about the EU weighing limits on social media for young children, not a health data deal in Asia.

tf.s: Australia brought in a ban on social media for children under 16.
tf.why: The story says the trend kicked off in Australia, which brought in a ban for anyone under 16.

tf.s: The EU wants to shut out all teenagers over 13 from social media forever.
tf.why: The ban would be for children under 13. After that age, teenagers would gradually be allowed to join once platforms are safer.

tf.s: Under the plan, children under 13 could still freely sign up for any social media app.
tf.why: False. Under the new idea, children under 13 would not be able to sign up for social media at all.

tf.s: Ursula von der Leyen heads up the European Commission.
tf.why: The story says von der Leyen heads up the European Commission and supports the plan.

tf.s: Everyone goes along with the EU's plan without any worries.
tf.why: Not everyone goes along with the plans, and some experts warn that age checks could put people's privacy at risk.

tf.s: The EU may make companies turn off features like autoplay for young users.
tf.why: The story says the EU may make companies turn off features like autoplay and endless scrolling.
